issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking restoration of possession after unlawful dispossession is confined to determining prior possession and does not determine title or a better right to possession.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a summary suit seeking restoration of possession of a flat and an office after alleging that they had been dispossessed.
The parties disputed whether the plaintiffs had been in possession of the properties before the alleged dispossession.
issues.conclusion: In a suit of this kind, title and better rights to possession are not for adjudication; the relevant issue is whether the plaintiff was in possession at some time within six months before filing the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides a summary remedy for a person unlawfully dispossessed and is intended to discourage extra-legal self-help. The Court noted that Section 6(3) bars an appeal or review from a decree in such a suit, referring to P.S. Sathappan (Dead) by Lrs. v. Andhra Bank Ltd. & Ors. (2004) 11 SCC 672 in discussing the procedural context.

predicates.summary_dispossession_proceeding: The plaintiff brought a summary proceeding seeking restoration after alleged unlawful dispossession.
predicates.dispute_concerns_prior_possession: The parties dispute whether the plaintiff possessed the property before the alleged dispossession.

issues.definition: When a summary proceeding seeks restoration after alleged dispossession and the dispute concerns prior possession, the decision does not determine title or a better right to possession.

issues.legal_issue: Courts deciding interim relief should assess practical justice and the parties’ competing risks rather than automatically refusing to decide matters that overlap with the merits of the suit.
material_facts: The interim dispute concerned possession of the same properties whose possession was at issue in the suit.
The suit had not been finally decided, and the interim dispute had reached the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: Courts should decide interim matters when necessary, while considering whether relief can rest on issues distinct from the main suit, whether partial relief would suffice, and the consequences to each party if relief is granted or refused; interim relief amounting to a pre-trial decree should be avoided where possible.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that the practical realities of delay make strict neutrality or automatic refusal to decide an interim matter impracticable. It directed courts to weigh the consequences for both parties, consider partial relief, and exercise judicial discipline when interim findings overlap with issues for trial.

predicates.interim_relief_proceeding: A court is deciding an application for relief before the main proceeding has been finally determined.
predicates.interim_issues_overlap_with_trial: The issues relevant to interim relief are connected with issues that will be decided at trial.
predicates.immediate_relief_is_needed: The circumstances call for a decision on relief before the main proceeding is finally determined.

issues.definition: When interim relief is sought and the issues overlap with trial or immediate relief is needed, the court should balance the parties’ competing consequences and consider whether limited relief will suffice.

issues.legal_issue: An interlocutory mandatory injunction requires a stronger showing than a prohibitory injunction and is governed by the requirements of a strong case, prevention of serious or irreparable injury, and a balance of convenience.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought an interim direction requiring possession of the properties to be handed back to them.
The trial judge found the plaintiffs’ entitlement to interim restoration seriously doubtful in light of inconsistencies and improbabilities in their case.
The High Court appellate bench granted the plaintiffs interim possession through a mandatory direction.
issues.conclusion: Interim mandatory relief requires the highest degree of satisfaction, including a strong case for trial, the need to prevent serious or irreparable injury, and a balance of convenience in favour of the applicant.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Dorab Cawasji Warden v. Coomi Sorab Warden and Others (1990) 2 SCC 117, which states that an interlocutory mandatory injunction generally requires a case stronger than the prima facie case for a prohibitory injunction, necessity to prevent irreparable or serious injury, and a favourable balance of convenience; the ultimate decision remains a matter of judicial discretion.

rule.if: interim_mandatory_injunction_sought and strong_case_for_trial and serious_or_irreparable_injury_without_relief and balance_of_convenience_favours_applicant

predicates.interim_mandatory_injunction_sought: A party asks the court, before final judgment, to order another party to take a positive step or restore a prior state of affairs.
predicates.strong_case_for_trial: The applicant's case is stronger than the ordinary prima facie showing required for a prohibitory injunction.
predicates.serious_or_irreparable_injury_without_re: The applicant would suffer serious or irreparable injury that ordinarily cannot be compensated with money if relief is withheld.
predicates.balance_of_convenience_favours_applicant: The practical balance of convenience favours the party seeking the injunction.

issues.definition: An interim mandatory injunction may be granted when it is sought on a strong case, is needed to prevent serious or irreparable injury, and the balance of convenience favours the applicant.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not replace a trial court’s discretionary decision on interim relief merely because it would have reached a different conclusion if the matter had been before it initially.
material_facts: The trial judge considered the parties’ documents and found inconsistencies and improbabilities that required determination at trial, declining interim restoration of possession.
The appellate bench considered the same documents differently and granted interim mandatory relief.
The Supreme Court found that the trial judge’s view was a possible view and that the appellate bench had not shown it to be palpably incorrect or untenable.
issues.conclusion: The appellate bench should not have interfered with the trial judge’s discretionary order; the Supreme Court set aside the appellate order and restored the trial judge’s order, without expressing an opinion on the merits of the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Wander Ltd. v. Antox India (P) Ltd. 1990 (Supp) SCC 727, an appellate court reviewing discretion should not reassess the material and substitute its own conclusion where the trial court’s view was reasonably possible. Interference is justified where discretion was exercised arbitrarily, capriciously, or perversely, or settled principles were ignored. The Court also referred to Printers (Mysore) Private Ltd. v. Pothan Joseph and Charles Osenton & Co. v. Jhanaton on appellate review of discretionary decisions.

predicates.appeal_from_interlocutory_discretionary_: A party appeals an interlocutory order in which the trial court exercised discretion.
predicates.trial_court_view_reasonably_possible: The trial court's conclusion was a view reasonably open to it on the material before it.
predicates.trial_court_discretion_arbitrary_or_perv: The trial court exercised its discretion arbitrarily or perversely, or ignored settled legal principles.

issues.definition: On an appeal from an interlocutory discretionary order, an appellate court should not substitute its own discretion when the trial court’s view was reasonably possible and its discretion was not arbitrary or perverse.
